kurz: Why the financial industry measures risk as fluctuation, while investors usually take it to mean a loss, and which risks the volatility figure does not capture.

bloecke.md:
Two people talking about risk can mean different things by it. One measures how much a price fluctuates. The other asks whether the money will still be there in twelve years' time, when the property has to be paid for. Both questions are legitimate, but only the first can be expressed precisely in a single number. That is why this number appears in every prospectus.

The financial industry has agreed to measure risk by the standard deviation of returns, usually called [[Volatility|volatility]]. This choice is a convention. It has a practical advantage and a weakness that lies in the method of calculation itself.

bloecke.erklaerung: The standard deviation measures how far, on average, the individual annual returns deviate from the mean. Upward and downward deviations are given equal weight.
variablen: standard deviation, usually as a percentage per year
arithmetic mean of all annual returns
bloecke.beispiel: MSCI World (net, in euros), 1970-2025: mean 9.6%, sigma 19.5%.

bloecke.md:
## What a standard deviation of 19.5% tells you

From 1970 to 2025, calculated net in euros, the MSCI World returned an arithmetic mean of 9.6% a year with a standard deviation of 19.5%. If annual returns were normally distributed, around two thirds of all years would lie between minus 9.9% and plus 29.0%. Of the 56 years, 39 fell within this range, or 70%. As a rough guide, the figure is therefore usable.

In detail, however, its limits become apparent. Only 16 of the 56 years were between plus 5% and plus 15%, and thus close to the average. Nine years brought more than plus 30%, five years less than minus 20%. The average return is a calculated value, and most individual years were well above or below it.

bloecke.titel: Distribution of annual returns of the MSCI World (net, euros), 1970-2025
bloecke.unter: The annual returns do not cluster around the mean. The worst year (minus 37.6%) lies further from the mean than the best (plus 45.7%), so the distribution extends further to the left than to the right.

bloecke.md: The standard deviation treats upward and downward swings alike. The year 1999, with plus 45.7%, increases it, as does 2008 with minus 37.6%. Yet nobody calls a gain of 45% a risk. Volatility therefore says nothing about harm.

Volatility can only be measured where prices are formed continuously. Investments without a daily market, such as closed-end funds, unlisted property or private equity, are valued by appraisers, and appraisals smooth out performance. The low volatility figure of such products is therefore often a consequence of infrequent valuation and not evidence of low uncertainty. With an index fund traded daily, by contrast, fluctuation is fully visible, without the fund being any more dangerous as a result.

## Three risks that volatility does not capture

The first of these risks is **permanent loss of capital**. A price fall that recovers is above all a strain on the nerves. A loss that does not recover, on the other hand, permanently reduces wealth. Whether a fall turns into a permanent loss depends on whether there is still a functioning business behind the security and who owns the security if things go wrong. A certificate is a bearer bond (Inhaberschuldverschreibung). If the issuer becomes insolvent, the investor only has an insolvency claim and receives at most a pro rata share of the issuer's insolvency estate. The assets of a UCITS fund, by contrast, are held by a depositary separately from the assets of the fund management company. For German funds set up as segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen), these assets expressly do not form part of the fund management company's insolvency estate if it becomes insolvent (Section 99(3) KAGB, German Investment Code). No volatility figure reveals this difference.

The second risk is **concentration**. At the end of August 2026, the USA accounted for 72.1% of the MSCI World's index weight, the information technology sector for 29.8% and the ten largest constituents for 26.6%. The volatility of past decades gives no indication of how heavily the result of the next ten years depends on a few American corporations.

The third risk is the **duration of loss periods**. Besides the question of how deep a fall goes, how long it lasts also matters.

bloecke.titel: Underwater curve of the MSCI World (net, euros), year-end levels 1969-2025
bloecke.unter: The curve shows the distance from the highest year-end level reached so far. By the end of 2025, 100 had grown to around 6,414. The area below the zero line shows the loss periods that investors had to endure during this time.

bloecke.md:
## Drawdown and the duration of loss periods

The maximum [[Drawdown|drawdown]] is the largest fall from a peak to a trough before a new peak is reached. In the daily data from 2001 onwards, the largest fall of the MSCI World in euros is minus 53.6%, measured from 24 May 2001 to 9 March 2009. At the end of 1999, the index stood even higher; from that year-end level to 9 March 2009, it lost around 55%. On the coarser year-end basis of the chart, the figures were minus 52.5% at the end of 1974, after two consecutive years of losses, and minus 45.9% at the end of 2008.

The duration of a fall weighs more heavily than its depth. After the peak at the end of 1999, the index stood below that level for thirteen consecutive year-ends, and only in 2013 was there a new peak. During the oil crisis, the index stayed below its peak from the end of 1972 until the end of 1980, so for eight year-ends. In real terms, that is, in terms of purchasing power, US equities returned minus 0.8% a year from 1966 to 1981 and also minus 0.8% a year from 2000 to 2012. Such periods exceed the patience of most investors and the time frame of many investment plans.

The data also show the other side, however. From 1970 to 2025, all 42 rolling fifteen-year windows of the MSCI World were positive, the weakest at plus 1.8% a year. Of the ten-year windows, by contrast, 5 out of 47 were negative, the worst being 2000 to 2009 at minus 3.8% a year. The time horizon is thus itself a risk parameter. This statement is based on past observations and is no promise for the future.

The last row of the table shows the US money market. In 98 years, it did not have a single year that was negative in nominal terms, and it returned 3.4% a year; US equities returned 10.0%. The difference of around 6.6 percentage points a year is the equity risk premium. The market pays it as compensation for investors enduring the fluctuations and losses shown in the right-hand columns. Investors who avoid fluctuation forgo this premium. That does not make them free of risk, because their risk shifts from fluctuation to purchasing power.

bloecke.text: Risk means more things can happen than will happen.
bloecke.quelle: Elroy Dimson, quoted in Howard Marks, The Most Important Thing

bloecke.md: Howard Marks and Warren Buffett do not equate risk with fluctuation. They define it as the probability of a permanent loss of capital and purchasing power. The drawback of this definition is that it cannot be measured in advance, because it asks about the probability of a state that occurs only once. Its advantage is that it asks about what harms investors. Volatility can be observed but is only partly relevant. A permanent loss is relevant but cannot be observed in advance. Neither quantity replaces the other.

## Risk capacity and risk tolerance

**[[Risk capacity]]** is objective and can be calculated. It indicates how much loss a household can bear without getting into financial difficulties. The deciding factors are the investment horizon, the stability of income, the size of the savings buffer, fixed costs and debts, and whether your own income is linked to the portfolio. An investor holding shares in their own employer loses income and portfolio value at the same time if things go wrong.

**[[Risk tolerance]]** is subjective. It describes how much loss someone can endure without selling. It is hard to establish in advance by asking, because people are braver in a questionnaire than in a real crash such as the one in March 2020. Your own behaviour in the last downturn is more telling than any self-assessment test.

The two quantities are independent of each other, and this independence gives rise to the typical mistakes.

bloecke.titel: Risk capacity and risk tolerance as separate axes
bloecke.unter: The equity allocation is always based on the smaller of the two quantities and not on their average.

felder.text: Wants risk, cannot bear it. A short horizon and no buffer force sales at the worst moment.
Long horizon, stable income, composure. Only here can a high equity allocation be justified.
No buffer, little tolerance. First the emergency fund and expensive debts, then choose asset classes.
Could bear it, cannot stand it. A smaller allocation that is stuck to is better than being talked into more.

bloecke.md: The legislature also distinguishes between the two quantities. Under Section 64(3) WpHG (Securities Trading Act), an investment services firm providing investment advice must ask about both the investment objectives, including risk tolerance, and the financial situation, including the ability to bear losses. The recommended investment must match both. Investors without an adviser carry out this check themselves. It therefore remains necessary but is not documented for anyone.

bloecke.titel: Summary risk indicator in the key information document
bloecke.md:
In the EU, every packaged investment product for retail investors requires a key information document (PRIIPs KID). Since the beginning of 2023, this has also applied to retail funds and ETFs, which previously used the older KIID. The document contains a [[Summary risk indicator (SRI)|summary risk indicator]] on a scale from 1 to 7. It combines a market risk measure based on past VaR-equivalent volatility with a credit risk measure for the issuer's ability to pay. This is set out in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/653, Annexes II and III.

The indicator provides a rough classification of historical fluctuation and default risk that is comparable across the EU. It says nothing about valuation levels, concentration, costs or the duration of a loss period. A 2 therefore stands for a low-volatility investment, not a safe one. Low-volatility investments lose purchasing power in any case as soon as their interest rate is below the inflation rate.

Volatility describes how much the value has fluctuated along the way. Risk concerns whether the investment goal is achieved. A portfolio is correctly structured if its fluctuation matches what the household can bear and the investor can endure. Low fluctuation alone is not enough for this.

schritte.titel: Set a horizon for each goal
schritte.text: For each purpose, note the year in which the money will be needed. Money firmly earmarked for use within five years does not belong in volatile investments, however calm you feel.
Check whether there is a savings buffer covering three to six months of expenses and no expensive consumer debt. Without a buffer, the account balance determines the time of sale, not risk tolerance.

schritte.titel: Write down the loss in euros
schritte.text: Instead of “minus 50%”, write down the amount. With a portfolio worth €40,000, that is €20,000. A percentage remains abstract, an amount does not, and only the amount triggers the reaction that matters.

schritte.titel: Choose the equity allocation by the smaller quantity
schritte.text: Set the equity allocation so that the calculated amount remains bearable even in the historically worst case. A smaller allocation that is held achieves more than a large one that is sold.

mitnehmen: Volatility is the standard deviation of returns; it weights upward and downward swings equally and thus measures the strength of fluctuations, but not harm.

In euros, the MSCI World had a standard deviation of 19.5% a year from 1970 to 2025, fell by more than half at times, and after the 1999 high stood below its old level for thirteen consecutive year-ends.
Permanent loss of capital, concentration in the index and the duration of loss periods are not contained in the volatility figure.
Low measured volatility can also result from prices being determined only rarely.
Risk capacity results from a calculation about the household, risk tolerance is a characteristic of the investor, and the smaller of the two quantities determines the equity allocation.

begriffe.text: The standard deviation of returns, usually on an annual basis. It measures dispersion both upwards and downwards and says nothing about the direction, cause or duration of a fall.
The percentage fall from the previous peak. The maximum drawdown is the deepest of these falls before a new peak is reached.
A household's objective ability to bear losses. It results from the investment horizon, income stability, savings buffer, fixed costs and debts.
The subjective willingness to endure fluctuations without selling. It only shows itself reliably in a real downturn, not in a questionnaire.
A mandatory indicator from 1 to 7 in the key information document, derived from historical fluctuation (market risk measure) and the issuer's default risk (credit risk measure).
